use /lib
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/project-locations import ProjectLocationsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope

from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope

export scope ContainerEnvironmentScope:
    concept: {ContainerEnvironmentConcept}

concept ContainerEnvironmentConcept:
    pitch:
        A container the application owns, that a run of the harness works
        in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or
        change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its
        prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't
        read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it
        tries.

    shape: {ContainerEnvironmentShape}

shape ContainerEnvironmentShape:
    description:
        Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and
        questions from the Ask tab always run in a container, and are the
        only runs that do. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code step always
        run on the host, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, with their
        protected locations, and never need Podman. Freeform tasks always
        run on the host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the
        palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt
        titles, which change nothing.

        Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on
        the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's
        snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes
        commits there, as ever.

    runtime:
        The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command,
        and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's
        command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its
        standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as
        a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its
        container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.

        On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user,
        with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the
        user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its
        containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

    missingPodman:
        Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a
        container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task,
        a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed
        does, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, or as one whose spec
        build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to
        run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's
        installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

        - on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
        - on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
        - on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

        A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and
        runs whether it is installed or not.

    podmanMachine:
        On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is
        running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and
        offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs
        `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is
        one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a
        button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`.
        Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it
        runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending
        it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux
        there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

export scope ContainerEnvironmentScope:
    concept: {ContainerEnvironmentConcept}

concept ContainerEnvironmentConcept:
    pitch:
        A container the application owns, that a run of the harness works
        in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or
        change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its
        prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't
        read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it
        tries.

    shape: {ContainerEnvironmentShape}

shape ContainerEnvironmentShape:
    description:
        Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and
        questions from the Ask tab always run in a container, and are the
        only runs that do. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code step always
        run on the host, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, with their
        protected locations, and never need Podman. Freeform tasks always
        run on the host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the
        palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt
        titles, which change nothing.

        Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on
        the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's
        snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes
        commits there, as ever.

    runtime:
        The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command,
        and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's
        command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its
        standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as
        a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its
        container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.

        On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user,
        with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the
        user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its
        containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

    missingPodman:
        Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a
        container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task,
        a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed
        does, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, or as one whose spec
        build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to
        run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's
        installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

        - on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
        - on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
        - on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

        A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and
        runs whether it is installed or not.

    podmanMachine:
        On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is
        running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and
        offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs
        `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is
        one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a
        button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`.
        Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it
        runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending
        it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux
        there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

    podmanAccess:
        Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is
        running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container
        for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is
        missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its
        service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because
        of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or
        any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed.
        The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and
        failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it
        prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or
        question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run
        because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written,
        what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead.
        The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for
        that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that
        the build failed.

    image:
        Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`,
        and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness
        commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the
        version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its
        latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions
        changes.

        Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The
        build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as
        `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built
        against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which
        command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't
        run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run
        `piton build` to check its work.

        A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own,
        `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what
        its runs in a container need, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says. The
        project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when
        the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the
        project's runs use the default image.

        While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows
        "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes
        to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

    mounts:
        What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing
        else from the host. The project is mounted at the same fixed path in
        the container, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, on every platform, each location given
        at its place relative to the project directory under `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`,
        and the run works in `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`. So a harness that keys its
        sessions on its working directory, as Claude Code does, finds them
        again after the project moves, whatever its path on the host. What
        each kind of run is given, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} names
        the locations, follows.

        spec:
            A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the
            spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the
            harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can
            run `piton build` itself; the fluency file, read only;
            piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file,
            read and write. Never the code location.

        question:
            A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec
            location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read
            only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container. Nothing is
            writable but the harness's own volume and the questions' sessions
            folder. Where one of the code location and the spec location
            holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither
            is hidden from the question by the other.

        Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read
        and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.

        Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the
        user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the
        project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code
        location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without
        the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it, unless
        the run is given the one held as well, as a question is given both
        the code location and the spec location.

        A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history
        folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file
        has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just
        before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not
        written yet is.

    paths:
        On every platform, every path a run reports from its container is
        mapped back to its host path, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl` standing for the project
        directory, before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec
        in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its
        understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls
        touched. Only a path that is `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, or begins with
        `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl/`, is mapped, never text that merely holds it, as
        `/workspace-old`. A path
        that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and
        opens nothing.

    volumes:
        The only volumes are one per harness, for its login and settings,
        ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness
        keeps it, owned and named by the application and shared by every
        project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them. Losing
        one costs only a login.

        The harness's sessions are never kept in a volume. They are kept in
        the project, in `.suspense/sessions/`, as the @{ProjectDataScope}
        says, one folder per conversation: `spec` for the spec lane's, and
        `questions` for the Ask tab's questions. Each run mounts only its own
        conversation's folder, read and write, where the harness keeps its
        sessions under its home, as Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects, never
        `.suspense/sessions/` as a whole, so no run sees another
        conversation's sessions. The application creates the folder before
        the run if it isn't there. So a conversation carries on across runs,
        restarts of the application, and moves of the project, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says.

        Losing the project's sessions folder costs only the conversations'
        context: the next run starts a new conversation, as when a session
        can't be resumed. Sessions kept in volumes before this aren't carried
        over; each conversation starts fresh.

    loggingIn:
        When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs
        its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows
        a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the
        command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's
        browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has
        a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where
        the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port
        is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a
        device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is
        sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is
        cancelled or fails.

        The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed
        there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every
        run. The @{SettingsWindowScope} shows whether each harness is logged
        in in its container, and can log it in again.

    guards:
        A run in a container has no protected locations, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} names them: it isn't guarded, and its
        harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location,
        since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, name only what it can see. Runs on
        the host keep their protected locations as ever.

    specBuild:
        A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work
        in the refreshed reference; with no code location there, what that
        build writes into the code location, the shape's guidance, goes
        nowhere. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over,
        however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as
        the @{SpecBuildScope} says, so the host's reference and shape guidance
        are those of the spec as the run left it.

        in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or
        change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its
        prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't
        read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it
        tries.

    shape: {ContainerEnvironmentShape}

shape ContainerEnvironmentShape:
    description:
        Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and
        questions from the Ask tab always run in a container, and are the
        only runs that do. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code step always
        run on the host, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, with their
        protected locations, and never need Podman. Freeform tasks always
        run on the host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the
        palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt
        titles, which change nothing.

        Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on
        the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's
        snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes
        commits there, as ever.

    runtime:
        The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command,
        and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's
        command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its
        standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as
        a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its
        container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.

        On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user,
        with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the
        user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its
        containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

    missingPodman:
        Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a
        container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task,
        a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed
        does, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, or as one whose spec
        build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to
        run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's
        installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

        - on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
        - on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
        - on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

        A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and
        runs whether it is installed or not.

    podmanMachine:
        On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is
        running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and
        offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs
        `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is
        one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a
        button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`.
        Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it
        runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending
        it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux
        there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

    podmanAccess:
        Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is
        running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container
        for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is
        missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its
        service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because
        of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or
        any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed.
        The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and
        failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it
        prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or
        question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run
        because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written,
        what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead.
        The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for
        that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that
        the build failed.

    image:
        Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`,
        and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness
        commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the
        version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its
        latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions
        changes.

        Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The
        build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as
        `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built
        against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which
        command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't
        run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run
        `piton build` to check its work.

        A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own,
        `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what
        its runs in a container need, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says. The
        project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when
        the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the
        project's runs use the default image.

        While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows
        "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes
        to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

    mounts:
        What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing
        else from the host. The project is mounted at the same fixed path in
        the container, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, on every platform, each location given
        at its place relative to the project directory under `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`,
        and the run works in `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`. So a harness that keys its
        sessions on its working directory, as Claude Code does, finds them
        again after the project moves, whatever its path on the host. What
        each kind of run is given, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} names
        the locations, follows.

        spec:
            A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the
            spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the
            harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can
            run `piton build` itself; the project's `.piton` directory, which
            holds the build's manifest of the files it owns, read and write,
            for the same reason; the fluency file, read only;
            piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file,
            read and write. Never the code location: in its place, an empty
            scratch directory, writable, that nothing else sees and that goes
            with the container, so `piton build` finds the code location it
            places the shape's guidance in.

        question:
            A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec
            location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read
            only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container. Nothing is
            writable but the harness's own volume and the questions' sessions
            folder. Where one of the code location and the spec location
            holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither
            is hidden from the question by the other.

        Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read
        and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.

        Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the
        user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the
        project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code
        location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without
        the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it, unless
        the run is given the one held as well, as a question is given both
        the code location and the spec location.

        A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history
        folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file
        has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just
        before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not
        written yet is.

    paths:
        On every platform, every path a run reports from its container is
        mapped back to its host path, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl` standing for the project
        directory, before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec
        in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its
        understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls
        touched. Only a path that is `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, or begins with
        `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl/`, is mapped, never text that merely holds it, as
        `/workspace-old`. A path
        that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and
        opens nothing.

    volumes:
        The only volumes are one per harness, for its login and settings,
        ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness
        keeps it, owned and named by the application and shared by every
        project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them. Losing
        one costs only a login.

        The harness's sessions are never kept in a volume. They are kept in
        the project, in `.suspense/sessions/`, as the @{ProjectDataScope}
        says, one folder per conversation: `spec` for the spec lane's, and
        `questions` for the Ask tab's questions. Each run mounts only its own
        conversation's folder, read and write, where the harness keeps its
        sessions under its home, as Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects, never
        `.suspense/sessions/` as a whole, so no run sees another
        conversation's sessions. The application creates the folder before
        the run if it isn't there. So a conversation carries on across runs,
        restarts of the application, and moves of the project, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says.

        Losing the project's sessions folder costs only the conversations'
        context: the next run starts a new conversation, as when a session
        can't be resumed. Sessions kept in volumes before this aren't carried
        over; each conversation starts fresh.

    loggingIn:
        When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs
        its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows
        a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the
        command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's
        browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has
        a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where
        the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port
        is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a
        device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is
        sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is
        cancelled or fails.

        The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed
        there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every
        run. The @{SettingsWindowScope} shows whether each harness is logged
        in in its container, and can log it in again.

    guards:
        A run in a container has no protected locations, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} names them: it isn't guarded, and its
        harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location,
        since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, name only what it can see. Runs on
        the host keep their protected locations as ever.

    specBuild:
        A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work
        in the refreshed reference; with no code location there, what that
        build writes into the code location, the shape's guidance, goes
        nowhere. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over,
        however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as
        the @{SpecBuildScope} says, so the host's reference and shape guidance
        are those of the spec as the run left it.

use /lib
from ../project-data import ProjectDataScope
from ../project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
from ../prompt-mode/ask-conversation import AskConversationScope
from ../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from ../prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from ../settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
from ../user-preferences import UserPreferencesScope
from ./baked-prompts import BakedSystemPromptsScope
from ./catalog import HarnessCatalogScope

from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope

export scope HarnessIntegrationScope:
    concept: {HarnessIntegrationConcept}

concept HarnessIntegrationConcept:
    pitch:
        Uses the one-off version of a coding harness for the selected
        ${ProjectDirectoryScope}: `claude -p`, `codex exec`, or `opencode run`,
        whichever the user chose. Each run carries on a conversation, so the
        harness keeps its context between requests.

    shape: {HarnessIntegrationShape}

shape HarnessIntegrationShape:
    description:
        Should always run in auto mode.

        The project's system prompt, its system template filled in, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, is appended to the harness's own
        system prompt, for example with `--append-system-prompt`, the same for
        every prompt of a conversation whatever its mode. The compiled
        systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor, its mode's instructions,
        heads the prompt's own message instead.

        The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the
        harness does is streamed back as it happens. A task's run takes its
        prompt as a stream of messages rather than a single one, so it can be
        fed more while it works, as its feeding says.

        Its directory, which a system prompt's HARNESS_DIRECTORY stands for,
        is that of the harness in use: .claude, .codex, or .opencode.

        Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and
        questions always run the harness in a container the application owns,
        as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says, which holds only what their
        mode may use. Every other run, Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code
        step, always, with their protected locations, Freeform, and the
        application's own, runs the harness on the host, in the project directory. Either
        way the harness is run, prompted, and read just as this says.

    harnesses:
        The harness in use is the one picked in the @{SettingsWindowScope}:
        Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode, Claude Code until another is picked.
        It is remembered for the user, as the @{UserPreferencesScope} says, not
        for a project. Every run the application starts goes to it, the tasks,
        the questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the
        notes, commit messages, and prompt titles it writes, and everything
        else works the same whichever it is. A run already going when another is picked
        finishes with the harness it started with, and a conversation is only
        carried on by the harness it began with; the next request with another
        harness starts a new one.

        Each harness is run its own way, streaming what it does as a line of
        JSON per event, which is read into the same reply, tool calls, usage,
        and result, whichever harness wrote it:

        - Claude Code is `claude -p`, in auto mode, the system prompt given
            with `--append-system-prompt`, a conversation carried on with
            `--resume`, and a copy of one with `--fork-session`.
        - Codex is `codex exec`, with `--full-auto` and `--json`, the prompt
            read from its standard input, a conversation carried on with
            `resume`.
        - OpenCode is `opencode run`, with `--format json`, a conversation
            carried on with `--session`.

        Codex and OpenCode take no system prompt of their own, so it is given
        ahead of the prompt, marked off from it. Neither can carry on a copy of
        a conversation, so a question asked while another is running starts a
        new conversation with them instead. The notes, commit messages, and
        prompt titles are written with a small model where the harness can be
        told one, Claude Code's haiku, and with the harness's default model otherwise.

        When the harness picked isn't installed, a run on the host fails
        saying that it can't be run, as any run that can't be started does. A
        run in a container uses the harness in its image instead, and fails,
        where Podman isn't installed or can't run, as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says.

    protectedLocations:
        Only a run on the host has protected locations. A run in a container
        has none, since nothing it mustn't touch is mounted there, as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says: it isn't guarded, and its harness is
        given no rule against reading or editing anything.

        Where the harness takes rules for what its tools may do, as Claude
        Code does with `--disallowedTools`, a run on the host is told what its
        mode keeps it off. A Code task is told it may not edit the spec location, and a
        Spec task the code location; the application puts back whatever
        changes there all the same, and says so in the task's output as a
        passive notice, never an error, as the @{TaskTableScope} says. A Code
        task is also told it may not read the spec location, alongside that,
        so it reads the compiled reference instead, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says. A question from the Ask tab always
        runs in a container, so it is never given this rule, nor any other
        telling it to keep off the spec location. This rule is only a nudge, and
        doesn't enforce anything, since a shell command can still read the
        files, and nothing puts anything back or stops the run when one does. A harness that
        takes no such rules is told nothing of either.

    feeding:
        A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code
        with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of
        JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as
        the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt,
        as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the
        @{ChatInputScope}, is written as another.

        A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather
        than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that
        call is over. The harness echoes each message back as it takes it in,
        with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is
        answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under
        way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.

        A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its
        turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the
        background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background
        task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its
        kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet
        ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started,
        and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended
        as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is
        matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run
        when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.

        A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is
        the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no
        background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while
        a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still
        going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays
        open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's
        input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the
        harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the
        state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps
        running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task
        as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its
        input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the
        background, since its whole process group is ended with it.

        Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt
        and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either
        takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.

        Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes,
        commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

    images:
        Images attached to a prompt, as the @{ChatInputScope} says, are given
        to the harness as it takes them: to Claude Code as image content blocks,
        base64-encoded with their media type, in the same stream-json user
        message as the prompt's text, after it; to Codex with an `--image`
        argument per image; and to OpenCode with a `--file` argument per image.
        A message fed to a running Claude Code task carries its images the same
        way, and a Claude Code run that isn't fed more but has images is given
        its prompt as a stream-json message too, so the images can go with it.
        Codex's options end with `--` before the prompt when it is given
        images. Questions take images as tasks do.

    context:
        The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh
        each time. Each lane of the @{PromptSendingScope} carries on a
        conversation of its own, so nothing a task of one lane read reaches a
        task of the other: the spec lane's, carried on by Spec tasks and a
        Chain prompt's spec steps, and the code lane's, carried on by Code
        tasks, a Chain prompt's code step, and Freeform tasks. Each task sent
        carries on its own lane's, and since a lane runs one task at a time,
        two tasks never carry on the same conversation at once. A Chain
        prompt's steps hand on to each other as text, the prompt and what the
        step before replied, as the @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, so the
        handoff crosses lanes whatever each lane's conversation holds. When
        the project is opened, each lane carries on the latest conversation
        among its own tasks in the history, a Chain task by the lane of the
        step it was.

        The spec lane and the questions always run in a container, and the
        code lane always on the host, so each conversation is only ever
        carried on where it began. A run in a container keeps its
        conversation's sessions in the project, in its own folder of
        `.suspense/sessions/`, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says, so
        it carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of
        the project; a run on the host keeps them where the harness keeps
        them on the host.

        Questions from the Ask tab share a separate
        conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on
        the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question
        asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation,
        so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A
        conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open
        project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is
        in the background. A spec lane or questions conversation from before
        its sessions were kept in the project, whose session the project's
        sessions folder doesn't hold, is still tried, and when the harness
        has no such session, the request is sent again at once as a new
        conversation, as below.

        A request whose conversation can't be carried on, because the
        harness says it has no such session, as Claude Code's "No
        conversation found", or because it was begun elsewhere, is never
        failed for it, and never retried on the same conversation: it is
        sent again at once as a new conversation, the same prompt, with no
        context, and the conversation it couldn't carry on is not tried
        again by any later request, the project's history included. A
        question sent again so is recorded and shown as starting a new
        conversation, as the @{AskConversationScope} marks one. Each run applies
        its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation
        begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts
        fresh.

        A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New
        conversation button, as the @{ChatInputScope} says, which leaves the
        conversation of the lane it is used for: the next request in it
        starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not
        carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's
        history. Leaving it is kept with the project, as the @{ProjectDataScope}
        says, so a project opened after a lane's or the questions' conversation
        was left starts a new one there too, rather than carrying on the latest
        conversation in its history, until a run after the reset begins one of
        its own. How much context a conversation holds is
        known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the
        model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest
        reply; replies of subagents don't count.

    failures:
        A run that fails always says what went wrong, in the harness's own
        words: the error its result carries, or the error events it
        streamed, and where it gave none, what it printed on its standard
        error, and its exit status, as written. A task shows it in its
        output and a question at the end of its answer. It never reads
        only "the harness reported an error", or any other message that

concept HarnessIntegrationConcept:
    pitch:
        Uses the one-off version of a coding harness for the selected
        ${ProjectDirectoryScope}: `claude -p`, `codex exec`, or `opencode run`,
        whichever the user chose. Each run carries on a conversation, so the
        harness keeps its context between requests.

    shape: {HarnessIntegrationShape}

shape HarnessIntegrationShape:
    description:
        Should always run in auto mode.

        The project's system prompt, its system template filled in, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, is appended to the harness's own
        system prompt, for example with `--append-system-prompt`, the same for
        every prompt of a conversation whatever its mode. The compiled
        systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor, its mode's instructions,
        heads the prompt's own message instead.

        The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the
        harness does is streamed back as it happens. A task's run takes its
        prompt as a stream of messages rather than a single one, so it can be
        fed more while it works, as its feeding says.

        Its directory, which a system prompt's HARNESS_DIRECTORY stands for,
        is that of the harness in use: .claude, .codex, or .opencode.

        Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and
        questions always run the harness in a container the application owns,
        as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says, which holds only what their
        mode may use. Every other run, Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code
        step, always, with their protected locations, Freeform, and the
        application's own, runs the harness on the host, in the project directory. Either
        way the harness is run, prompted, and read just as this says.

    harnesses:
        The harness in use is the one picked in the @{SettingsWindowScope}:
        Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode, Claude Code until another is picked.
        It is remembered for the user, as the @{UserPreferencesScope} says, not
        for a project. Every run the application starts goes to it, the tasks,
        the questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the
        notes, commit messages, and prompt titles it writes, and everything
        else works the same whichever it is. A run already going when another is picked
        finishes with the harness it started with, and a conversation is only
        carried on by the harness it began with; the next request with another
        harness starts a new one.

        Each harness is run its own way, streaming what it does as a line of
        JSON per event, which is read into the same reply, tool calls, usage,
        and result, whichever harness wrote it:

        - Claude Code is `claude -p`, in auto mode, the system prompt given
            with `--append-system-prompt`, a conversation carried on with
            `--resume`, and a copy of one with `--fork-session`.
        - Codex is `codex exec`, with `--full-auto` and `--json`, the prompt
            read from its standard input, a conversation carried on with
            `resume`.
        - OpenCode is `opencode run`, with `--format json`, a conversation
            carried on with `--session`.

        Codex and OpenCode take no system prompt of their own, so it is given
        ahead of the prompt, marked off from it. Neither can carry on a copy of
        a conversation, so a question asked while another is running starts a
        new conversation with them instead. The notes, commit messages, and
        prompt titles are written with a small model where the harness can be
        told one, Claude Code's haiku, and with the harness's default model otherwise.

        When the harness picked isn't installed, a run on the host fails
        saying that it can't be run, as any run that can't be started does. A
        run in a container uses the harness in its image instead, and fails,
        where Podman isn't installed or can't run, as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says.

    protectedLocations:
        Only a run on the host has protected locations. A run in a container
        has none, since nothing it mustn't touch is mounted there, as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says: it isn't guarded, and its harness is
        given no rule against reading or editing anything.

        Where the harness takes rules for what its tools may do, as Claude
        Code does with `--disallowedTools`, a run on the host is told what its
        mode keeps it off. A Code task is told it may not edit the spec location, and a
        Spec task the code location; the application puts back whatever
        changes there all the same, and says so in the task's output as a
        passive notice, never an error, as the @{TaskTableScope} says. A Code
        task is also told it may not read the spec location, alongside that,
        so it reads the compiled reference instead, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says. A question from the Ask tab always
        runs in a container, so it is never given this rule, nor any other
        telling it to keep off the spec location. This rule is only a nudge, and
        doesn't enforce anything, since a shell command can still read the
        files, and nothing puts anything back or stops the run when one does. A harness that
        takes no such rules is told nothing of either.

    feeding:
        A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code
        with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of
        JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as
        the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt,
        as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the
        @{ChatInputScope}, is written as another.

        A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather
        than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that
        call is over. The harness echoes each message back as it takes it in,
        with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is
        answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under
        way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.

        A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its
        turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the
        background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background
        task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its
        kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet
        ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started,
        and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended
        as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is
        matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run
        when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.

        A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is
        the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no
        background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while
        a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still
        going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays
        open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's
        input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the
        harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the
        state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps
        running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task
        as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its
        input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the
        background, since its whole process group is ended with it.

        Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt
        and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either
        takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.

        commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

    images:

        to the harness as it takes them: to Claude Code as image content blocks,
        base64-encoded with their media type, in the same stream-json user
        message as the prompt's text, after it; to Codex with an `--image`
        argument per image; and to OpenCode with a `--file` argument per image.
        A message fed to a running Claude Code task carries its images the same
        way, and a Claude Code run that isn't fed more but has images is given
        its prompt as a stream-json message too, so the images can go with it.
        Codex's options end with `--` before the prompt when it is given
        images. Questions take images as tasks do.

    context:
        The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh
        each time. Each lane of the @{PromptSendingScope} carries on a
        conversation of its own, so nothing a task of one lane read reaches a
        task of the other: the spec lane's, carried on by Spec tasks and a
        Chain prompt's spec steps, and the code lane's, carried on by Code
        tasks, a Chain prompt's code step, and Freeform tasks. Each task sent
        carries on its own lane's, and since a lane runs one task at a time,
        two tasks never carry on the same conversation at once. A Chain
        prompt's steps hand on to each other as text, the prompt and what the
        step before replied, as the @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, so the
        handoff crosses lanes whatever each lane's conversation holds. When
        the project is opened, each lane carries on the latest conversation
        among its own tasks in the history, a Chain task by the lane of the
        step it was.

        The spec lane and the questions always run in a container, and the
        code lane always on the host, so each conversation is only ever
        carried on where it began. A run in a container keeps its
        conversation's sessions in the project, in its own folder of
        `.suspense/sessions/`, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says, so
        it carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of
        the project; a run on the host keeps them where the harness keeps
        them on the host.

        Questions from the Ask tab share a separate
        conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on
        the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question
        asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation,
        so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A
        conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open
        project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is
        in the background. A spec lane or questions conversation from before
        its sessions were kept in the project, whose session the project's
        sessions folder doesn't hold, is still tried, and when the harness
        has no such session, the request is sent again at once as a new
        conversation, as below.

        A request whose conversation can't be carried on, because the
        harness says it has no such session, as Claude Code's "No
        conversation found", or because it was begun elsewhere, is never
        failed for it, and never retried on the same conversation: it is
        sent again at once as a new conversation, the same prompt, with no
        context, and the conversation it couldn't carry on is not tried
        again by any later request, the project's history included. A
        question sent again so is recorded and shown as starting a new
        conversation, as the @{AskConversationScope} marks one. Each run applies
        its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation
        begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts
        fresh.

        A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New
        conversation button, as the @{ChatInputScope} says, which leaves the
        conversation of the lane it is used for: the next request in it
        starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not
        carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's
        history. Leaving it is kept with the project, as the @{ProjectDataScope}
        says, so a project opened after a lane's or the questions' conversation
        was left starts a new one there too, rather than carrying on the latest
        conversation in its history, until a run after the reset begins one of
        its own. How much context a conversation holds is
        known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the
        model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest
        reply; replies of subagents don't count.

        why it couldn't, and one Podman couldn't run says so, as the

content.text:
You're right that the fluency isn't injected, but that's by design and it isn't what's breaking the spec. The spec says the fluency is never part of the system prompt. Instead, the Spec and Chain instructions point at `.suspense/fluency.md`, which is mounted into the container. That worked in this session: I got the pointer and read the file.

**Why the spec keeps breaking:** a containerized run has no working way to check its own edits.

1. **`piton` couldn't run at all.** On my earlier steps today the image had glibc 2.36 and the `piton` binary needs 2.39, so every `piton` command failed. The runs edited blind. That's how a run left `locations:` alone on a prose line, which made `piton check` report `empty-value` at `container-environment/index.pi:127`. The image is now on Debian 13, and `piton` runs.
2. **`piton build` still can't succeed in the container, however sound the spec is.** It reports 75 errors that have nothing to do with the spec:
   - 73 are `unowned-output`. The `.piton/manifest.json` that records which reference files Belay owns isn't mounted, so piton refuses to overwrite them.
   - 2 are `unplaceable-instruction`. There's no code location for the shape guidance to go in.
